summary: Defines how to send IPv6 packets over PPP links, including the network control protocol used to set it up and configure it. It was replaced by RFC 2472.

eli5.summary: It teaches an old phone-line connection how to carry the new kind of internet addresses and get both ends ready.

questions: how do ppp links get ipv6 addresses
subtitle: Sending new-format internet addresses over point-to-point links.

tldr.problem: Internet addresses were changing from IPv4 to IPv6, but Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) links like dial-up modems did not know how to handle the new address format.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2023 defines how to wrap IPv6 packets in PPP frames, and introduces IPv6CP, a control protocol that both ends of a PPP link use to negotiate settings and configure IPv6.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was replaced by RFC 2472, which obsoletes its approach.

today: RFC 2023 was obsoleted by RFC 2472, which updated the approach to IPv6 over PPP.

sections.title: Introduction and the PPP Layers
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) is a way to send data over serial connections like modems. It has three main layers: a method for wrapping data into frames, a control protocol for setting up the link itself (LCP), and network control protocols (NCPs) for setting up specific network protocols like IPv6.

RFC 2023 defines the NCP for IPv6, called IPv6CP. Before any IPv6 packets can travel across a PPP link, the connection must first reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase, and IPv6CP must negotiate and open.
sections.eli5: PPP works in layers. The bottom layer is the cable or phone line, the middle layer sets up the connection, and the top layer says "now we will speak IPv6 here."

sections.title: Sending IPv6 Packets
sections.content: Each IPv6 packet is wrapped in exactly one PPP frame, with a protocol field value of hex 0057 to mark it as IPv6 data. The maximum length of an IPv6 packet on a PPP link is the same as the maximum PPP frame size. PPP links carrying IPv6 must support at least 576 octets in each frame's data section.
sections.eli5: IPv6 packets fit inside PPP envelopes, like letters in an envelope. The envelope is marked to say what is inside.

sections.title: IPv6CP: The Control Protocol
sections.content:
IPv6CP mirrors the structure of LCP (the PPP link control protocol) but is specific to IPv6. It uses the same packet types: Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, Configure-Reject, Terminate-Request, Terminate-Ack, and Code-Reject. IPv6CP packets are marked with protocol field hex 8057. Both ends must negotiate settings and reach the Opened state before IPv6 traffic can flow.

The protocol field value for IPv6CP is 8057 (hex), and it only uses Codes 1 through 7; other codes trigger a Code-Reject.
sections.eli5: Before they send IPv6, the two ends of the link swap messages saying "I am ready for IPv6, are you?" and agree on the details.

sections.title: Configuration Options
sections.content:
IPv6CP has two configuration options. The Interface-Token option negotiates a unique 32-bit value for each end of the link; this token is later used in IPv6 address autoconfiguration. The IPv6-Compression-Protocol option lets both ends agree on compression, though compression is off by default. Each end must request compression separately if it wants bidirectional compression.

The Interface-Token should be a random non-zero value. If a good random source is not available, an implementation may suggest a zero token and let the peer provide a different one. Both ends must choose different tokens; if they cannot negotiate unique tokens, recovery is not specified (manual configuration may be needed).
sections.eli5: The two ends negotiate two things: a unique number for each side (so they do not get confused), and whether to squeeze the data smaller with compression.

sections.title: Link-Local Addresses and Autoconfiguration
sections.content: IPv6 addresses on PPP links are built from a standard link-local prefix and the Interface-Token negotiated via IPv6CP. The link-local address format is: 10 bits of the prefix FE80::, 86 zero bits for padding, and the 32-bit Interface-Token. This means each PPP interface gets a unique link-local address without needing to detect address conflicts (duplicate address detection is skipped).
sections.eli5: The phone line gets an address built from a standard prefix and the unique number the two ends agreed on. Each side gets a different address automatically.
